properties.name: Bath
properties.one_line: The Romans built a temple and bathing complex over a natural hot spring that fed 1,170,000 liters of 46-degree water a day into a lead-lined reservoir. Dedicated to Sulis Minerva, a fusion of the local Celtic goddess and Roman Minerva, the site drew pilgrims from across Britannia seeking cures and cursing thieves on lead tablets thrown into the sacred spring.
properties.image_credit: Roman Baths, Bath · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Wiesbaden
properties.one_line: A garrison town grew up around 26 mineral springs on the edge of the Rhine frontier, first mentioned by Pliny the Elder around 77 CE for the heat of its waters. Auxiliary troops guarding the limes bathed here before it developed into a full spa settlement under the Flavians and Trajan.
properties.image_credit: Kochbrunnen pavilion over the thermal spring, Wiesbaden · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Pavilion built over the ancient Aquae Mattiacae spring, not a Roman-era structure itself

properties.name: Terme di Cotilia
properties.one_line: A sulfurous spring resort in the Sabine hills with a rock-cut pool 60 by 24 meters, favored every summer by the emperor Vespasian, who bathed in its cold waters and died there on 24 June 79 CE. His son Titus kept the family tradition of taking the cure at the same springs.
properties.image_credit: Roman bath ruins, Aquae Cutiliae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Acqui Terme
properties.one_line: Pliny the Elder praised the sulfur springs here as the most famous in Liguria, and the Romans built a bathhouse whose brick arches, the Bollente arcade, still carry near-boiling water into the town center today. The resort sat on the road linking Genoa to the Po valley, a convenient stop for travelers taking the cure.
properties.image_credit: La Bollente hot-spring fountain, Acqui Terme · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The modern fountain house over the ancient Aquae Statiellae spring

properties.name: Baden-Baden
properties.one_line: Roman soldiers stationed on the upper Rhine frontier built bathhouses over the hot springs here in the late first century CE, part of a small garrison settlement of around 8 hectares. The waters, still around 68 degrees Celsius at the source, would later draw emperors including Caracalla for their arthritis.
properties.image_credit: Roman bath ruins, Baden-Baden · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Aachen
properties.one_line: Legionaries channeled the hot sulfur springs at Büchel into a bathing complex at the start of the first century CE, later adding a second bath house, the Münstertherme, along with a forum and aqueducts. By Trajan's reign the settlement covered some 25 hectares and was being groomed for city status.
properties.image_credit: Elisenbrunnen pavilion, Aachen · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Neoclassical pavilion over the Roman-era thermal spring, not the Roman structure itself

properties.name: Chaves
properties.one_line: A garrison town on the Braga-Astorga road grew around hot springs that still surface at 73 degrees Celsius, one of the hottest in Europe. Its 140-meter, eleven-arch bridge over the Tamega, begun under Vespasian and finished under Trajan by 104 CE, still carries an inscription naming ten dependent tribal communities.
properties.image_credit: Roman baths of Chaves · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Aquae Calidae
properties.one_line: Thermal baths beside the Black Sea coast tapped hot springs that had already been in use for thousands of years before Rome arrived. The waters ran continuously through baths on this spot for over 1,700 years, later drawing emperors, Bulgarian khans, and an Ottoman sultan to the same basin.
properties.image_credit: Aquae Calidae on the Tabula Peutingeriana · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A detail of the ancient Roman road map showing the site, not a photograph

properties.name: Baden
properties.one_line: A spa settlement grew up beside the Limmat a few miles from the legionary camp at Vindonissa, its 47-degree waters credited with healing powers by soldiers and settlers alike. Tacitus described it as a small town valued above all for the pleasant setting of its warm springs.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological excavation in the Bäderviertel, Baden · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological dig in Baden's bath quarter, on the site of Aquae Helveticae

properties.name: Aix-en-Provence
properties.one_line: Founded in 122 BCE by the proconsul Gaius Sextius Calvinus around a warm mineral spring, this was the first Roman settlement in Gaul. Its baths, built in the later first century CE, drew on water still flowing today at a constant 33 degrees Celsius, prized for treating rheumatism and skin ailments.
properties.image_credit: Roman sarcophagus found at Aquae Sextiae · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A sarcophagus recovered from the site, not the baths themselves

properties.name: Varazdinske Toplice
properties.one_line: Roman settlers built a bathhouse, forum, and small capitol over sulfur springs already sacred to the local Iasi tribe, whose name gave the site its Latin title. The complex sat on the road network of southern Pannonia, drawing bathers to its warm, sulfurous pools through the second century and beyond.
properties.image_credit: Thermal baths at Aquae Iasae, Varaždinske Toplice · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Daruvar
properties.one_line: A bathing complex rose beside mineral-rich hot springs in Roman Pannonia, its warm and cold pools built for soldiers to rest and recover as well as for civilian bathers seeking relief from skin and joint ailments. Dedications found at the site name the local healing deities Sedatus and Silvanus alongside the springs.
properties.image_credit: Daruvarske toplice spa · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The modern Daruvar spa built over the ancient mineral springs of Aquae Balissae

properties.name: Bourbonne-les-Bains
properties.one_line: A shrine and bathing establishment grew around hot springs sacred to Borvo and Damona, Gallic healing deities the Romans absorbed rather than replaced. Sick visitors threw thousands of coins and inscribed lead tablets into the spring asking the gods for cures, many of which archaeologists later recovered from the basin.
properties.image_credit: Roman bath ruins, Bourbonne-les-Bains · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Gallo-Roman baths at Bourbonne-les-Bains

properties.name: Neris-les-Bains
properties.one_line: A spa town of some size took shape around mineral springs in the territory of the Bituriges Cubi, complete with an amphitheater seating several thousand for entertainment between treatments. More than 4,000 coins and dozens of carved gemstones recovered from its pools attest to centuries of grateful visitors.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Théâtre-amphithéâtre gallo-romain ("Parc des Arènes") à Néris-les-Bains (France, Allier).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Gallo-Roman amphitheatre, Néris-les-Bains · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The amphitheatre at the Gallo-Roman spa town of Néris-les-Bains, part of the same ancient site as the baths

properties.name: Dax
properties.one_line: A spa town developed under Augustus around hot springs that still discharge over 2 million liters of 64-degree water a day, among the most productive thermal sources in Gaul. Its baths served the Tarbelli tribe's chief settlement and travelers moving along the Atlantic coast road toward Hispania.
properties.image_credit: Gallo-Roman temple crypt, Dax · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The excavated temple crypt at the site, not a bathing hall

properties.name: Vicarello
properties.one_line: Pilgrims seeking cures at this spring on the shore of Lake Bracciano left behind one of the richest votive deposits in the Roman world: over 5,000 bronze coins and four inscribed silver cups mapping the entire road from Cadiz to Rome. The waters were dedicated to Apollo, patron of healing, and drew visitors for centuries.
properties.image_credit: Baths of Apollo, Vicarello · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rufus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: A physician trained in Alexandria who returned to practice in his home city, Rufus wrote influential treatises on anatomy, the pulse, gout, and jaundice that later doctors like Galen quoted at length. He was a contemporary of the physician Statilius Criton, who served Trajan, placing his career squarely in this reign.
properties.image_credit: Portrait of Rufus of Ephesus, engraving · Wellcome Collection / Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Archigenes of Apamea
properties.one_line: A Syrian-born physician who practiced medicine in Rome during Trajan's reign, Archigenes led the eclectic Pneumatic school and wrote on fevers, pulse diagnosis, and surgery for aneurysms. His detailed clinical descriptions of headache and vertigo symptoms were still being cited by physicians centuries later.
properties.image_credit: Great Colonnade at Apamea, Syria — Archigenes' hometown · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)
properties.image_alt: Roman colonnaded street at Apamea, Syria

properties.name: Soranus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: Trained in Alexandria and born in Ephesus, Soranus practiced medicine in Rome across the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, making him active in the capital in 117 CE. His four-book treatise on gynecology, covering pregnancy, midwifery, and infant care, remained the standard reference in the field for over a thousand years.
properties.image_credit: 9th-century manuscript page, Soranus's Gynaecology · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: The Museion and its associated medical faculty remained the dominant training ground for physicians across the Roman world, carrying forward a tradition of human dissection pioneered here by Herophilus and Erasistratus four centuries earlier. Physicians from Ephesus to Rome, including Soranus, traveled to Alexandria to study before setting up practice elsewhere.
properties.image_credit: The Great Library of Alexandria, 19th-century engraving by O. Von Corven · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Kos
properties.one_line: The birthplace of Hippocrates kept its name as medicine's founding school five centuries after his death, its teaching tradition built around careful bedside observation and the Hippocratic Corpus of case histories. Physicians across the empire still trained in the Hippocratic method that traced its roots to this island.
properties.image_credit: Tree of Hippocrates, Kos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The traditional site associated with Hippocrates's teaching, not a surviving Roman-era school building

properties.name: Cnidus
properties.one_line: A rival tradition to Kos across the water, the Cnidian school built its reputation on detailed classification of diseases by organ, producing the influential text known as the Cnidian Sentences. Its early physician Chrysippus of Cnidus trained Erasistratus, who went on to found the great anatomical school at Alexandria.
properties.image_credit: The twin harbours of ancient Knidos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The harbours of Knidos (Cnidus), Turkey, site of the rival Cnidian medical school

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Vespasian created the first state-funded teaching chairs in the capital in 71 CE and exempted physicians from billeting soldiers and paying taxes, formalizing medical practice as a protected profession. By Trajan's reign Rome hosted a resident community of prominent doctors, including Archigenes and Soranus, teaching and treating patients at the empire's political center.
properties.image_credit: Portrait of an unknown Roman doctor · Wellcome Collection / Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sanctuary of Asklepios at Epidaurus
properties.one_line: The most famous healing sanctuary in the Greek world drew the sick from every province to sleep in its abaton dormitory, where priests interpreted dreams as messages from Asklepios prescribing a cure. Nearly a thousand years after its founding, the sanctuary's theater, Tholos rotunda, and temple were still receiving pilgrims under Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: The Abaton (incubation hall), Sanctuary of Asklepios, Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Asklepieion of Kos
properties.one_line: Built on three rising terraces on a hillside outside town, this sanctuary paired temple worship with practical treatment rooms, medicinal spring-fed fountains, and Roman-era baths on its lowest level. Physicians here practiced as priests, treating patients in the tradition attributed to their most famous predecessor, Hippocrates.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Kos, panoramic view · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Asklepieion of Athens
properties.one_line: An Athenian citizen named Telemachos founded this sanctuary on the Acropolis's south slope in 420 BCE, bringing the cult of Asklepios to the city during a devastating plague. The complex held a sacred spring, an altar, and stoas for pilgrims, and remained in active worship on the same terrace beside the Theatre of Dionysos into the second century CE.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis south slope, Athens · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A general view of the south slope where the Asklepieion stood, not a close-up of the sanctuary

properties.name: Asklepieion of Corinth
properties.one_line: Set against the north city wall with a view over the Corinthian Gulf, this sanctuary combined a temple to Asklepios with an adjoining dining hall and a spring-fed courtyard where patients bathed as part of treatment. Terracotta votive offerings shaped like healed body parts, arms, legs, and eyes, still line the site's storerooms from centuries of grateful dedications.
properties.image_credit: Statuette of enthroned Asklepios, Archaeological Museum of Corinth · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A museum statuette from Corinth's Asklepieion, not a photo of the sanctuary ruins

properties.name: Temple of Aesculapius
properties.one_line: After a plague struck Rome in 293 BCE, priests fetched a sacred snake from Epidaurus to found this healing shrine; the animal swam ashore at this island and marked the spot itself. The Tiber Island temple, its edges carved to resemble a ship's prow in honor of the myth, still functioned as a center of healing in 117 CE and remains a hospital site today.
properties.image_credit: Tiber Island, Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A modern view of the island where the Temple of Aesculapius stood; no photo of the temple itself survives

properties.name: Pontine Marshes
properties.one_line: A belt of stagnant lowland south of Rome along the Via Appia bred malarial mosquitoes so persistently that the marsh blocked Roman expansion southward for centuries. Julius Caesar planned a drainage scheme that was never finished, and the swamp remained a byword for fever until Mussolini's engineers finally reclaimed it in the twentieth century.
properties.image_credit: Leonardo da Vinci's map of the Pontine Marshes, c. 1514–15 · Royal Collection / Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A Renaissance-era map of the marshes, used here for lack of an ancient depiction

properties.name: Sardinia's malarial coast
properties.one_line: Ancient DNA recovered from Roman-period burials on Sardinia's coast carries a genetic mutation that offers protection against malaria, confirming the disease was already entrenched on the island under Roman rule. The low coastal plains were considered so unhealthy that Rome used the island as a place of banishment, expecting the climate itself to punish exiles.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Fenicotteri sullo Stagno di Cabras al Tramonto.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Stagno di Cabras wetland, Sardinia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A coastal lagoon on Sardinia's west coast, part of the historically malarial wetland belt

properties.name: Etruria's coastal marshes
properties.one_line: Poor drainage along Etruria's coastal plain left standing water that bred fever-carrying mosquitoes across a stretch of lowland later known as the Maremma, contributing to the decline of once-thriving Etruscan port cities like Vulci and Vetulonia. Roman-era writers associated the coast's summer air with sickness long before the cause was understood.
properties.image_credit: Diaccia Botrona wetland reserve, Grosseto · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Modern remnant marshland in the Maremma, once part of Etruria's malarial coastal plain

properties.name: Buxton
properties.one_line: A Roman bathing establishment rose over Buxton's warm spring, dedicated to the local goddess Arnemetia and recorded in the Ravenna Cosmography as Aquis Arnemeza. Excavations in 1695 uncovered a lead-lined bath about 20 meters long beneath what's now the town's Georgian Crescent. Only Bath itself rivals Buxton among Roman Britain's confirmed spa towns.
properties.image_credit: Natural Mineral Baths building, Buxton · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The historic bath building over the Aquae Arnemetiae spring; no Roman-era masonry survives above ground

properties.name: Hammam Righa
properties.one_line: A Roman colonia grew up around these hot springs, complete with a forum, theater, library, and an aqueduct feeding its bathhouse. The name simply means hot waters -- one of several towns called Aquae Calidae scattered across the empire's Mediterranean provinces. The springs are still in use today, two thousand years on.
properties.image_credit: Hammam Righa, site of Aquae Calidae Caesaris · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Banos de Bande
properties.one_line: A Roman army camp for soldiers of Legio VII Gemina, built here around 75 CE while they cut the Via Nova through the mountains of Gallaecia, came with its own bathhouse, barracks, and granaries. The name preserves a local water-spirit cult the legionaries found already in place. Much of the site now sits under a reservoir and only surfaces when the water drops in drought years.
properties.image_credit: Open-air Roman baths, Aquis Querquennis, Baños de Bande · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Caldas de Reis
properties.one_line: A municipium on the Antonine Itinerary's road from Bracara Augusta to Asturica Augusta, marked in the road-book as the mansio de Aquis Celenis. Its hot springs also fed the start of a second route running up the coast. The modern town's name, Caldas, still just means hot springs in Galician.
properties.image_credit: Roman-era hoard found at Caldas de Reis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A treasure hoard recovered at the site, not a photo of the baths

properties.name: Alhama de Aragon
properties.one_line: The poet Martial, born in nearby Bilbilis, praised these sulphurous springs in his epigrams and recommended them to friends back in Rome. The site sat on the Antonine Itinerary's road network through the Ebro valley. Roman bath remains were reported here by antiquarians as early as the 19th century.
properties.image_credit: Thermal lake, Alhama de Aragón · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Hammam Essalihine
properties.one_line: Inscriptions here dedicate the bath complex to Vespasian and Titus, built around 76 CE not long after the two emperors returned from crushing the Jewish revolt. Septimius Severus's engineers would come back to repair it more than a century later. The spring has been in continuous use for close to two thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Roman baths at Aquae Flavianae, Hammam Essalihine · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Terme Taurine
properties.one_line: Republican-era bathers were already soaking in these sulphurous springs by 86 BCE, long before Trajan built his new harbor town of Centumcellae just down the coast. Trajan and then Hadrian expanded the baths considerably, likely as part of Trajan's own nearby villa. The ruins are now a public archaeological park.
properties.image_credit: Republic-era ruins, Terme Taurine · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Abano Terme
properties.one_line: Pliny the Elder, Suetonius, and Martial all wrote about the Fons Aponi, a spring hot enough -- around 80 degrees Celsius at its source -- to double as an oracle: dice thrown in were said to answer questions by how they landed. The waters still supply the modern spa town built over the site.
properties.image_credit: Entrance to the Montirone archaeological park, site of the Roman-era Fontes Aponi springs, Abano Terme · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Entrance to the Montirone archaeological park at Abano Terme

properties.name: Bagni di Tivoli
properties.one_line: Strabo and Pliny the Elder both described these sulphurous pools east of Rome, fed by springs so mineral-heavy they built their own travertine terraces over the centuries -- the same stone quarried nearby to build the Colosseum. Locals later nicknamed the ruins the Baths of Queen Zenobia.
properties.image_credit: The Aquae Albulae springs, Bagni di Tivoli · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Calan
properties.one_line: A thermal-bath vignette on the Tabula Peutingeriana marks this spot on the road network radiating from Sarmizegetusa, the new Dacian provincial capital Trajan founded after his conquest of 106 CE. A dedication to the 'Genius of the Aquae district' survives from a village nearby. Barely a decade old as Roman territory in 117 CE, but already plumbed into the empire's road system.
properties.image_credit: Roman thermal baths of Germisara, Geoagiu-Bai, Romania · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of Roman baths at Germisara, Dacia

properties.name: Bagneres-de-Luchon
properties.one_line: Strabo mentions these Pyrenean hot springs by name, and dozens of votive altars pulled from the Pique River confirm it -- local worshippers thanked the native water god Ilixo/Lixon for cures long before and after Rome arrived. Marble-lined pools with hypocaust heating have been excavated on the site.
properties.image_credit: Thermal baths building, Bagnères-de-Luchon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Capvern
properties.one_line: The Antonine Itinerary places a station of this name on the road running from Aquae Tarbellicae (Dax) to Tolosa (Toulouse), serving the Convenae, a tribe Rome resettled here from across the Pyrenees. Antiquarians identified the site with modern Capvern by matching the itinerary's distances.
properties.image_credit: Thermal baths building, Capvern-les-Bains · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The modern spa at Capvern, on the site the Antonine Itinerary places as a station of the Convenae

properties.name: Vichy
properties.one_line: A Roman settlement grew up at this river crossing in Arverni territory around a warm spring, on a road junction that made it a natural stopping point. It never rivaled the grand imperial spa towns of Italy or Gaul's own Aquae Sextiae, but the waters kept drawing visitors long after Rome fell, into the resort town Vichy is today.
properties.image_credit: Hall des Sources over the Célestins spring, Vichy · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A 19th-century structure built over the ancient Aquae Calidae spring, not a Roman ruin

properties.name: Mondragone
properties.one_line: Livy already mentions these springs during the Second Punic War, and Pliny the Elder recommended them as a cure for barrenness and mental illness centuries later. The emperor Claudius is recorded taking the waters here, on the Campanian coast a short distance from the more famous resort of Baiae.
properties.image_credit: Venus statue found at Sinuessa, Mondragone · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: A statue recovered from the site, not a photo of the baths

properties.name: Sasso di Furbara
properties.one_line: Strabo called this spring more crowded than the old Etruscan city of Caere itself, and a much later physician, Caelius Aurelianus, ranked its water the hottest in Italy. Rediscovered in 1987, the excavated pools still show their marble thresholds and mosaic floors.

properties.name: Hammam Bou Hanifia
properties.one_line: The Romans named this spring for the Sirens, and built a colonia around its waters west of Caesarea. It's one of a string of thermal towns along Mauretania Caesariensis's interior road network, most now known mainly by their still-operating modern hammams.
properties.image_credit: Hammam Bou Hanifia thermal baths · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The modern hammam at Bou Hanifia, built over the Roman-era Aquae Sirenses springs

properties.name: Sceaux-du-Gatinais
properties.one_line: A major Gallo-Roman pilgrimage sanctuary dedicated to the water goddess Segeta, with a monumental courtyard, colonnaded galleries, and a nymphaeum built around her sacred spring. Excavations continue at the site, protected as a French historic monument since 1986.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological remains of the Gallo-Roman sanctuary of Segeta (Aquae Segetae), Sceaux-du-Gâtinais, France · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Termini Imerese
properties.one_line: Founded in the late 1st century BCE, this colony took its name -- Warm Springs -- from waters the Greek poet Pindar had already praised five centuries earlier. Its forum, amphitheater, and aqueduct-fed baths served a town that outlasted the Greek city of Himera it grew up beside; part of the ancient caldarium is now built into a modern hotel.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/DSC00124 - Tubi di piombo romani - Foto di G. Dall'Orto.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Roman lead water pipes from the ancient baths at Termini Imerese, Sicily (Thermae Himerenses) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-era lead pipes from the bath complex; a modern hotel now stands over the ancient bath site

properties.name: Hammam Meskhoutine
properties.one_line: Named for its ties to the nearby Numidian town of Thibilis, this bath complex drew on some of North Africa's most striking travertine terraces, built up over millennia by mineral-saturated water. The remains today are scattered and weathered, but the springs themselves are still hot enough to cook an egg.
properties.image_credit: Travertine terraces, Hammam Meskhoutine (Aquae Traiani) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sardara
properties.one_line: Ptolemy and the Antonine Itinerary both mark a stop on the road between Othoca and Caralis at this spring in Sardinia's interior, where ruins dated to the 1st century BCE still stand in the town's municipal park. The island's Roman-era baths are far less famous than Italy's, but the water is real and still flowing.
properties.image_credit: Roman bath ruins, Sardara · Wikimedia Commons
